## Problem

Vimeo's blog hosted thousands of posts dating back to the early 2000s and ran on a legacy WordPress instance maintained by an outside contractor. It was completely separate from the rest of the marketing codebase - expensive to operate, difficult to maintain, and visually out of step with a company-wide rebranding effort underway at the time.

## Approach

I took on the migration end to end. The first step was a thorough audit of every custom block type in WordPress, mapping each one to an equivalent React component in the new headless CMS. The goal wasn't just a technical lift-and-shift, the new components also needed to align with Vimeo's updated design language and use the same component library as the rest of the marketing site.

Once the component mapping was complete, I wrote a data migration script to convert the full archive of posts to the new format. With thousands of posts and varying block configurations, content integrity was a primary concern throughout.

I also coordinated across multiple stakeholders: design, marketing, and the content team, keeping everyone aligned on scope and decisions as the project progressed.

## Outcome

The migration successfully moved Vimeo's entire blog archive to the headless CMS, consolidating two separate content management systems into one. Content editors gained a significantly improved authoring experience, the blog now shares the same component library as the rest of the marketing site, and annual operating costs were reduced.
Led the architecture of Vimeo's company-wide marketing design system, keeping Figma, Storybook, and the CMS in sync and building a TDD-first foundation that other engineers could build on.

## Problem

Vimeo's marketing site had no unified component system. Design worked in Figma, engineering worked in code, and the CMS had its own set of components, with nothing guaranteeing the three matched. The result was UI inconsistency, slower development, and no shared testing baseline for the components every marketing page depended on.

## Approach

Aligning on architecture before writing code. Before any implementation, I wrote a proposal comparing two structures: a colocated "capsule" approach, where each component owns its parts and variants in its own folder, and an atomic approach organized into atoms, molecules, and organisms. I presented both to the team to surface current pain points rather than push a single answer. We chose a mostly atomic structure because it mirrored how our designers organized components in Figma, which made parity between design and code far easier to maintain. From the capsule approach, we kept one idea: an optional `parts/` folder for pieces of a component that didn't warrant becoming an atom of their own.

```txt title="Capsule (colocated)"
Button/
├── Button.tsx
├── Button.stories.tsx
├── parts/
│   └── ButtonIcon.tsx
└── variants/
    └── PrimaryButton.tsx
```

```txt title="Atomic"
chroma/
├── atoms/
│   ├── Button/
│   └── Icon/
├── molecules/
│   └── SearchField/
└── organisms/
    └── Header/
```

```txt title="Hybrid (shipped)" mark={5,9,13} ins={14-15}
chroma/
├── atoms/
│   └── Button/
│       ├── Button.tsx
│       └── Button.stories.tsx
├── molecules/
│   └── SearchField/
│       ├── SearchField.tsx
│       └── SearchField.stories.tsx
└── organisms/
    └── Header/
        ├── Header.tsx
        ├── Header.stories.tsx
        └── parts/
            └── HeaderLogoLockup.tsx
```

### One source of truth across three tools

I worked in lockstep with Design to keep Figma specs, Storybook documentation, and Builder.io CMS components in parity, and overhauled our Storybook setup so it reflected exactly what designers specified and what marketers could use. I championed a test-driven approach, writing component tests directly in Storybook stories and running them with Storybook's built-in test runner. That made the documentation and the test suite the same artifact: every documented state was also a tested one, so the two could never drift apart.

### Decisions that keep a system healthy

Some of the most important work was deciding what not to do. As a team, we discussed whether to use barrel exports, since they make import paths much cleaner. Because Chroma lived in a monorepo, though, we decided against them over concerns about circular dependencies and bundle size, and relied on monorepo path aliases instead to keep imports readable. We added an ESLint rule to catch barrel exports early, so the decision would hold as more contributors joined.

```ts title="atoms/index.ts" caption="asdf"
export * from './Button/Button'
export * from './Icon/Icon'
export * from './Link/Link'
```

<small style="margin-top:-8px">Barrel exports</small>

```tsx title="atoms/Button/Button.tsx" del={1}
import { Icon } from '..' // resolves to atoms/index.ts, which re-exports Button itself
```

<small style="margin-top:-8px">Barrel imports</small>

```json title="tsconfig.json"
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "paths": {
      "@chroma/*": ["packages/chroma/src/*"]
    }
  }
}
```

<small style="margin-top:-8px">Path aliases</small>

### Scaling the people, not just the code

As other engineers joined, I onboarded them, guided them through component implementation, and served as the technical point of contact for the initiative.

### Bringing AI into the workflow

Later, I integrated the Figma MCP server so components could be scaffolded directly from design files, tightening design-engineering parity further. I also authored Claude Code rules files that encoded our coding standards, so AI-assisted contributions followed the same conventions as everything else in the system.

<Figure src={chromaFlow} alt="Workflow diagram: the Figma MCP server reads a Figma file for Claude Code, and a CLAUDE.md rule requires the Plop scaffolder, so every new component lands in Chroma the same way" />

### Governance built into creation

As more people, and more agents, contributed to Chroma, consistency couldn't depend on everyone remembering the conventions. I set up a Plop.js generator that scaffolded every new component the same way: placing it in the right atomic tier, creating its Storybook stories file, and generating the registration file that made it available in the CMS. To make sure AI contributions followed the same path, our CLAUDE.md rules file required agents to use the scaffolder rather than creating files by hand. Whether an engineer or an agent started a component, it was correct from the first commit, which kept code review focused on the component itself instead of catching drift.

## Outcome

Chroma became the foundation of Vimeo's marketing site: a single source of truth across design and engineering that improved component consistency, increased development velocity, and reduced UI defects. ## Problem

Vimeo needed a redesigned global navigation as part of a broader UX overhaul. Navigation sits at the top of every marketing page and has a direct relationship with conversion, so the stakes for getting it right were high, both visually and technically.

<Figure src={oldNavOpen} alt="Old Vimeo navigation with the Product menu open: a plain list of links with small icons, grouped under headings like Hosting and Player, Creation and Editing, and Platform" caption="Before" />
<Figure src={newNavOpen} alt="New Vimeo navigation with the Features menu open: the same groups, now with an icon tile and a one-line description for each item, plus a See all features link" caption="After" />

## Approach

I built the navigation as one of the first major components within Vimeo's [new marketing design system](/case-studies/chroma/), working closely with the UX designer throughout. One intentional decision that shaped the mobile implementation: rather than placing the navigation toggle at the top of the screen, the designer anchored it at the bottom. This was a deliberate ergonomic choice that makes one-handed use on a real device significantly more comfortable.

We launched as a controlled A/B test, starting with roughly 10% of traffic to limit risk. A stakeholder monitoring the results flagged a significant drop in mobile traffic to Vimeo's join page. I was brought into the cross-functional response, organizing a brainstorm sync with the UX designer, UI designer, and project manager. Rather than debating a single fix, we rapidly generated three distinct design directions to narrow faster. I implemented the winning approach, making the join button significantly more prominent on mobile, which not only recovered the lost traffic but produced a net lift to traffic on the primary conversion page.

Separately, after launch, a stakeholder flagged a performance issue: hovering over top-level navigation items caused a noticeable delay before dropdown menus appeared. I used Chrome's performance monitor to record and trace the interaction down the component tree. The culprit was a `useWindowResize` hook relying on a resize event handler, with many instances mounted simultaneously throughout the navigation. I replaced it with a new hook built on the browser's native `matchMedia` API, hoisted the listener to a single point higher in the tree, and passed the result down via React Context. This eliminated the delay entirely.

<Callout title="Did you know?">
  You can export the Chrome Performance profile and hand it to your AI tool of
  choice (mine's Claude). It's surprisingly good at narrowing down what's
  actually causing a slowdown like this.
</Callout>

## Outcome

The navigation launched successfully and now serves as a foundational piece of Vimeo's marketing UX. The A/B test process kept the initial blast radius small, the cross-functional collaboration turned a regression into a measurable win, and the performance fix removed a user-facing latency issue across the entire navigation surface.
